input:
## Start-up

Before you start the pump, you should take some time to prepare it properly. You should inspect both the pump and the motor, and you should confirm that the coupling guard is in place and that no tools or loose material have been left near the rotating parts. You should also check the bearing housing and confirm that the oil is standing at the mark on the sight glass. Where the coupling is accessible, you should turn the shaft by hand, and you should satisfy yourself that it turns freely, without any scraping or tight spots. If you find any defect at all, you should report it and leave the pump stopped until such time as the defect has been fully cleared.

The next stage is to fill the pump. You should open the vent at the top of the casing, and you should then open the suction valve slowly so that the suction line and the casing fill with liquid. You should keep the vent open until liquid that is free of air is flowing from the vent, at which point you should close the vent. It is worth remembering that a casing which still holds air will not deliver its discharge pressure, and the pump should on no account be started while it is in that state. You should also confirm that the discharge valve is closed, since a centrifugal pump is started against a closed discharge valve in order to keep the motor load low during the run-up period.

You may then start the motor. As the pump comes up to speed, you should watch the discharge pressure gauge carefully, as the pressure should rise promptly and then hold steady. Once the pressure has risen, you should open the discharge valve slowly and bring the flow up gradually, in stages. As the flow rises, you should check both the pump and the motor, looking for any leaks at the casing joints and at the seal, and listening for any scraping, rattling or knocking. If the pressure fails to rise, or if a leak opens up, or if abnormal noise or heat makes an appearance, you should stop the pump at once, and you should report the fault before any second attempt at starting is made.

## Normal operation

During normal operation, you should run the pump with a steady suction supply, and you should make sure that the casing remains full of liquid at all times. You should never run the pump dry, and you should never attempt to throttle the suction valve in order to control the flow. Flow should instead be controlled at the discharge valve, and every valve change that you make should be made slowly, because a fast change sends a pressure shock through the line which can damage both the pump and the pipework.

Throughout the shift, you should keep a watch on the discharge pressure and on the flow indication, both of which should hold near their normal values for the duty in hand. If the discharge pressure falls while the valves remain untouched, this points towards a loss of suction supply, a blockage, or wear inside the pump itself, whereas a rising pressure points towards a restriction downstream. You should treat either of these changes as a fault that is in the process of developing: you should reduce the flow, check the suction supply first, and report the change together with the readings that show it.

You should also make rounds of the pump at regular intervals, during which you should record the discharge pressure along with any other readings that the log requires. On each round, you should look for leaks at the joints, the flanges and the seal, and you should clear up any liquid that has been spilled. You should listen to the pump and to the motor, comparing the sound that you hear with the sound of the pump when it is in normal service, and you should check the bearing housing for heat and confirm that the oil mark is still showing on the sight glass. You should keep the area around the pump clear and dry, and you should report defects as and when you find them, since a defect that is reported early is merely a repair, whereas the same defect left running becomes a failure of the pump in service.

You should hand the pump over in a known state at the end of your shift. You should tell the next operator which duty the pump is on, whether there has been any change in its readings, and whether any defect is under report, and you should enter exactly the same points in the log. The next operator should not be left in the position of having to discover the state of the pump from the pump alone.

## Alarms

Two alarms are fitted to this pump, and each of them demands the action stated under it, in the order stated. On no account should you simply silence an alarm and carry on running the pump regardless.

Low suction pressure. This alarm comes into operation when the pressure at the pump suction falls below the level that the pump requires in order to stay full of liquid. When it acts, you should stop the pump and close the discharge valve. You should then check the suction supply and the suction line for a valve that has been left closed, a blockage, or a supply that has run empty. You should not restart the pump until the supply has been restored, the casing has been refilled and vented, and the suction pressure is standing normal while the pump is still stopped. You should report both the alarm and the cause that you found.

High bearing temperature. This alarm comes into operation when the temperature of a bearing rises above its normal working level. When it acts, you should stop the pump, and you should close the discharge valve followed by the suction valve. You should leave the pump to cool down, and you should not attempt to turn the shaft while the bearing remains hot. Once the pump is safe to approach, you should check the bearing housing for oil, and you should record the state of the oil exactly as you found it. You should not restart the pump until the cause of the heating has been found and cleared. You should report the alarm, together with the readings that were taken and the state in which the oil was found.

An alarm which acts without any fault being found should still be regarded as a fault in itself. You should report the alarm, the checks that were made and the readings that were taken, and you should leave the decision as to whether the pump returns to service to the supervisor on duty. You should, in addition, enter every alarm in the log, together with the action that was taken and the readings at the time, since the log entry forms part of the action rather than an optional addition to it.

## Shutdown

To shut the pump down, you should bring it down in broadly the reverse order of the start. You should close the discharge valve slowly, bringing the flow down in stages, and you should stop the motor once the discharge valve has been closed. You should then close the suction valve. At this point the pump will be standing full of liquid, isolated from the line on both sides.

You should next open the vent and confirm that the pressure within the casing has fallen away. In cases where the pump is going to be opened up, or where it will be standing out of service through a period of cold weather, you should drain the casing, and you should close the vent and the drain again once the draining has been completed. You should wipe up any liquid that has been spilled, bearing in mind that a pump which is left wet and dirty tends to hide the first signs of the next leak.

Where the stop is only a short one, and the pump will be returning to service on the same duty, you may leave the casing full and leave the valves exactly as they have been described above. Where the stop is a long one, you should drain the casing in the manner described. Whichever applies, the state in which the pump is left is the state that is recorded, and the start-up procedure should always begin from that recorded state rather than from memory.

You should leave the pump in a stated condition. You should record the shutdown in the log, including the state of the valves, whether or not the casing was drained, and any defect that is under report. You should tell the next operator the state of the pump at the handover. Where a pump is to be opened for work to be carried out, it must be handed over drained, vented and isolated, with its state entered in the log and stated at the handover, and no part of the pump is to be opened until that state has been confirmed by the person who will actually be doing the work.

## Alarms

Two alarms are fitted to this pump. Each alarm demands the action stated under it, in the order stated. Do not silence an alarm and continue to run the pump. Where both alarms act together, stop the pump first and work through both actions in full before any restart is considered.

Low suction pressure. This alarm acts when the pressure at the pump suction falls below the level the pump needs to stay full of liquid. Stop the pump. Close the discharge valve. Check the suction supply and the suction line for a closed valve, a blockage or an empty supply. Do not restart the pump until the supply has been restored, the casing has been refilled and vented, and the suction pressure stands normal with the pump still stopped. Report the alarm and the cause found.

High bearing temperature. This alarm acts when the temperature of a bearing rises above its normal working level. Stop the pump. Close the discharge valve and then the suction valve. Leave the pump to cool. Do not turn the shaft while the bearing is hot. Check the bearing housing for oil once the pump is safe to approach, and record the state of the oil as found. Do not restart the pump until the cause of the heating has been found and cleared. Report the alarm, the readings taken, and the state of the oil.

Enter every alarm in the log, with the action taken and the readings at the time. The log entry is part of the action, not an addition to it.

## Shutdown

Bring the pump down in the reverse order of the start. Close the discharge valve slowly and bring the flow down in stages. Stop the motor once the discharge valve is closed. Close the suction valve. The pump now stands full of liquid, isolated from the line on both sides.

Open the vent and confirm that the pressure in the casing has fallen. Drain the casing where the pump is to be opened, or where it will stand out of service through cold weather. Close the vent and the drain when draining is complete. Wipe up any spilled liquid. A pump left wet and dirty hides the first signs of the next leak.

For a short stop, with the pump returning to service on the same duty, the casing may be left full and the valves left as stated above. For a long stop, drain the casing as described. In both cases the state left is the state recorded, and the start-up procedure begins from the recorded state, not from memory.

Leave the pump in a stated condition. Record the shutdown in the log: the state of the valves, whether the casing was drained, and any defect under report. Tell the next operator the state of the pump at handover. A pump that is to be opened for work must be handed over drained, vented and isolated, with its state entered in the log and stated at the handover. No part of the pump is to be opened until that state has been confirmed by the person who will do the work.

The procedures of this chapter share one discipline. The pump is started full, run full and stopped in a stated order; its state at every handover is recorded; and every departure from the normal state is reported with the readings that show it, at the time it is found.
